The note describes that PISA estimates are accompanied by uncertainty (e.g., 95% confidence intervals) and that PISA technical standards were met in Brazil, implying the use of PISA’s complex survey methodology in the underlying database. The factsheet itself does not specify the exact weight variable names (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, so analysts should use the official PISA 2022 weights provided in the OECD PISA database when reproducing estimates. Because this is a descriptive reporting document (not an ML modeling paper), plausible values and survey design handling are expected to follow PISA’s standard scaling/estimation procedures rather than ad hoc ML-specific weighting.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Brazil factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in Brazil performed in mathematics, reading, and science, and how results evolved over time (notably 2018–2022 and longer trends since 2009). PISA 2022 used two two-hour tests with different students receiving different item sets, plus a student background questionnaire and a school principal questionnaire; the factsheet reports proficiency levels (e.g., Level 2 baseline, Levels 5–6 top performers) and subgroup patterns such as socioeconomic gradients and gender differences. In Brazil, average performance in all three domains is below the OECD average, and only 27% reached at least Level 2 in mathematics (OECD average: 69%), with 1% at Levels 5–6. The factsheet also reports that the mathematics gap between top and bottom deciles narrowed from 2018 to 2022, driven by improvements among low achievers and declines among high achievers. Methodologically, the document is descriptive and does not provide an explicit ML pipeline, PV-combining rule, or missing-data procedure; it instead relies on PISA’s standard scaling and uncertainty estimation documented elsewhere.
